1058.title: Christ the King
1058.hook: the last Sunday of the church year: a king crowned with thorns
1058.howItsDone: Catholic and some Protestant churches keep Christ the King on the last Sunday before Advent, with readings about Christ's kingship and hymns that call him king, and some end the service with a procession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Remembrance: poppies, silence, and swords beaten into plowshares. Your line was we will remember. Whose name did you stop to read? Day one thousand fifty-eight.

A soldier is twisting thorn branches into a ring, carefully, so it holds its shape. Around him, the rest of the band are laughing. They have found a scarlet robe. Someone has a reed for a scepter. The prisoner is already beaten and tired, and they are about to crown him. This is a joke. A whole coronation, staged as a joke, in a governor's hall in Jerusalem. On the last Sunday of the church year, before Advent starts the circle again, Catholic and some Protestant churches keep a feast for the man under those thorns. Today's word: Christ the King.
screen: `A SOLDIER TWISTS A RING OF THORNS.`
`THE LAST SUNDAY OF THE CHURCH YEAR.`

segments.voice: Look at what the soldiers do, piece by piece. Matthew tells it, in the King James words: "And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!" Crown, scepter, robe, a bended knee, a royal greeting. Every part of a real coronation is there. The soldiers mean all of it as mockery. Christians say the joke was true, and the soldiers didn't know it. Then the sign. John says Pilate wrote a title and had it put on the cross: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Meant as a charge. Read by Christians as a proclamation. Earlier that same morning, Pilate had asked Jesus straight out whether he was a king. And Jesus answered: "My kingdom is not of this world." Not that it isn't real, Christians say, but that it doesn't come from here, and doesn't run on the same rules. Its king doesn't send soldiers. He washes feet. In Mark, Jesus says he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life. So this feast turns a crown upside down. Paul, writing to the church at Philippi, says Jesus took the form of a servant, went all the way down to death on a cross, and that God lifted him high, so "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow." Notice the gesture. The soldiers bowed the knee to mock him. Paul says every knee should bow, this time in earnest. Same motion, opposite meaning. That's the feast: a different king, crowned with thorns, ruling by serving.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow to the servant king, or simply bow your head. Settle, and breathe. Picture the ring of thorns, the reed, the soldiers laughing. Then picture someone in your own life who served without a crown: a nurse on a night shift, a parent at a sink, a neighbor who shoveled your path. Slowly lower your head. If you pray, you can bow to Christ the King with Paul's words, at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. If you don't, let the bow be thanks for everyone who serves. The bell holds the time.
Christ the King. The feast on the last Sunday of the church year for a king crowned with thorns, whose kingdom is not of this world.
Your line: a different king. Today, do one small job nobody will thank you for, and do it on purpose. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: Thanksgiving
1059.hook: in North America, a harvest thanks at the table
1059.howItsDone: Some Christian families in the United States and Canada say grace before the Thanksgiving meal, sometimes holding hands, and some churches hold a Thanksgiving service or gather food for neighbors in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ the King: a crown of thorns, and a kingdom not of this world. Your line was a different king. What small job did you do on purpose? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

The ship has been driven by a storm for fourteen days. No sun, no stars. The cargo has gone over the side. The sailors have just been caught trying to slip away in the lifeboat. It's the dark before dawn, and nobody aboard has eaten properly since the storm began. Then one prisoner, a tentmaker called Paul, speaks up in the middle of it, takes a loaf of bread, and does something completely ordinary. He says grace. A strange place to begin a day about Thanksgiving, the holiday when, in North America, families sit down to a harvest meal and give thanks at the table. But that storm is where today starts. Today's word: Thanksgiving.

Here is Acts, in the King James words. Paul urges them all to eat, and then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Notice what he doesn't wait for. The storm isn't over. The ship hasn't reached land. He gives thanks in the middle, in front of terrified people, and the next verse says: "Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat." One person's grace turned into everyone's breakfast. Paul's grace has a pattern behind it. In Mark's Gospel, with a hungry crowd in the wilderness, Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to his disciples to set before the people. In Luke, two friends at Emmaus only recognize the risen Jesus when he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it. More than once in the Gospels, the meal begins with thanks. A letter in Paul's name puts the idea plainly: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Creature there means every created thing. The potatoes count. And to the church at Thessalonica, Paul wrote: "In every thing give thanks." Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing. In the storm, too. So at a Thanksgiving table, when someone says grace over a harvest meal, the words change from house to house. Some use the Psalms: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever." Some say a grace their grandmother said. Some just hold hands for a moment. The shape is the same as on that ship: stop, give thanks out loud, then eat together.
screen: `JESUS TOOK THE LOAVES AND GAVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say grace before a meal, or get ready to. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next meal you'll eat, and where you'll be. Then think of one thing in your life that isn't settled yet, a storm still going. Don't try to solve it. Just let it be there, the way the storm was there for Paul. Now choose a few plain words of thanks you could say before that meal anyway. If you pray, you can use a grace your family knows, or the psalm's line: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good. If you don't, just choose the words, and the breath you'll pause for before you eat. The bell holds the time.
Thanksgiving. In North America, a harvest meal with thanks at the table. In the Bible, giving thanks in every thing, even in the middle of a storm.

Your line: for all good gifts. Before your next meal, stop for one breath and give thanks out loud, even if something in your day is still unsettled, the way Paul did on the ship. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: St Andrew (30 November)
1060.hook: the first called, the one who brought his brother, near the start of Advent
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the story and the circle
1060.howItsDone: Churches that keep saints' days remember Andrew on the thirtieth of November, and in Scotland, where he is patron saint, the day is also kept as a national celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thanksgiving: Paul taking bread in the storm and giving thanks in front of everyone. Your line was for all good gifts. Where did you stop to give thanks? Day one thousand sixty.

"What seek ye?" In John's Gospel, in the King James words, that is the question Jesus turns round and asks two men who have been walking behind him. Their teacher, John the Baptist, had just pointed at him and said, "Behold the Lamb of God!" So they followed. They don't have a clever answer. They ask where he's staying. He says, "Come and see." And they spend the rest of that day with him. John's Gospel names one of the two. His name is Andrew. And the next thing Andrew does is go and look for his brother. The church keeps his day on the thirtieth of November, near the start of Advent. Today's word: St Andrew.

Here's what John says Andrew did after that day: "He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. And he brought him to Jesus." First findeth. Before anything else, he gets his brother. Jesus is about to give that brother, Simon, a new name: Cephas, a stone. We know him as Peter. And John calls Andrew simply Simon Peter's brother. In the Orthodox tradition, Andrew is called the First-Called, because in John's telling he is following Jesus before Peter ever arrives. Now watch what Andrew keeps doing. A huge crowd on a hillside, nothing to eat, and the disciples are worried. It's Andrew who notices a boy: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" He doesn't solve the problem. He just brings the boy, and the little he has, to Jesus. Later, in Jerusalem, some Greeks come asking to see Jesus. They ask Philip. Philip goes and tells Andrew. And Andrew and Philip go and tell Jesus. Three scenes: a brother, a boy, a group of strangers. In each one, Andrew is bringing someone. There John's story of him ends. Tradition says he traveled far to preach and died on a cross shaped like an X, and that cross now sits on the flag of Scotland, where he's the patron saint. His day falls near the start of Advent, which fits him. The season of waiting opens with the man who said, we have found him, and went to get someone else.

Here's the practice: bring someone to something good. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing you've found: a walk, a choir, a quiet church, a book, a kitchen table where people are kind. Then think of one person who might need it. Not the person who'd be easiest to ask. The one who came to mind first. Picture yourself asking, plainly, the way Andrew said, come and see. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
St Andrew. Simon Peter's brother, the one who kept bringing people to Jesus, remembered on the thirtieth of November.
Your line: we have found him. Today, invite one person to one good thing you've found. A walk, a song, a place. Just ask, and let them say no. Day one thousand sixty.

1061.title: Year three close: the story and the circle
1061.hook: a long line from Jericho to Lagos, and a year that keeps turning
1061.howItsDone: Western churches that follow the church year mark its turning at Advent (the Orthodox year begins on 1 September), and some end the old year with Christ the King and begin the new one with the first Advent candle, telling the same story again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Andrew, who found his brother and brought him. Your line was we have found him. Who did you invite to something good? Day one thousand sixty-one.

Twelve stones, piled up near Jericho. Each was carried up out of a river on a man's shoulder, from the dry riverbed where the priests stood, one man for each tribe. Joshua tells them the stones are for the children. That was near the start of this year: Israel crossing the Jordan. From there the story ran a long line, through judges and kings, exile and return, apostles and martyrs, monks and reformers, all the way to churches in Lagos. Then the line bent into a circle, and walked the church's year of feasts, from Advent candles to a king crowned with thorns. Today, both close. Today's word: Year three close.

This year had two shapes. The first was a line. Israel's story from Joshua to the return from exile. The early church, its martyrs and its creeds. The middle centuries, east and west: cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague. The reformations, Protestant and Catholic, with saints and failures on both sides. Then the church spreading across the world, to Lagos and far beyond. A line has a direction. It says: this happened, then this, and it matters what came first. The second shape was a circle. For these last weeks we walked the church year: Advent and Christmas, Lent and Easter, Pentecost, saints' days, All Souls, Christ the King. A circle doesn't go anywhere. It comes round again. In Western churches, the first Advent candle will soon be lit again. Ecclesiastes knew both shapes: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever." The generations are the line. The earth, and its seasons, are the circle. Go back to those stones by the Jordan. Joshua says they are a sign, so that "when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?" someone will tell them the story. That's how the line keeps going: a child asks, and someone answers. And that's why the circle matters: every year the feasts come round, the questions get asked again, and the story gets told again. The psalm puts it in one breath: "One generation shall praise thy works to another." Neither shape is finished. The line hasn't ended. The circle keeps turning. And somewhere on both of them, there's a spot marked today.

Here's the practice: write your place in the story. Settle, and breathe. Let the year pass by: the river and the stones, the prophets, the apostles, the monks, the reformers, the churches in Lagos, the candles and feasts. Then ask where you are in it today. Inside it, beside it, at the door, still deciding. All of those are places. Find one honest sentence that says where you stand. When the bell ends, write it down. If you pray, you can offer that sentence to God. If you don't, just keep it. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. The end of the long story: a line from Jericho to Lagos, and a circle of feasts that keeps turning.

Your line: the circle turns. Put your sentence somewhere you'll find it next year, like a stone by the river. Tomorrow, year four begins: many rooms, and how people talk about God. Day one thousand sixty-one.
